introScreens.headline: What Really Happened on Mars in 2018
introScreens.bodyText: In late May 2018, a NASA spacecraft orbiting Mars spotted a small swirling dust storm. Within three weeks, high-altitude winds whipped it into a monster storm wrapping around the entire planet—rising more than 37 miles high, seven times higher than an airplane flies on Earth. Dust blocked 97% of the sunlight so noon looked pitch black. NASA's solar-powered Opportunity rover ran out of battery in the dark and never woke up, while Curiosity kept working using a small nuclear battery.
introScreens.nasaSource: NASA Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter & Mars Exploration Rover Mission Archives (2018)

introScreens.headline: NASA's Next Big Step: Sending Humans to Mars
introScreens.bodyText: Through the Moon to Mars program, NASA is preparing the first human missions to live and work on the Red Planet. Real astronauts will need nonstop electricity every Martian Sol to create breathable oxygen, keep living quarters warm in -90°F nights, and keep liquid rocket fuel cold for their flight home. Because global dust storms erupt every few Mars years, NASA knows human bases cannot survive on solar panels alone.
introScreens.nasaSource: NASA Moon to Mars Architecture & Fission Surface Power Studies

introScreens.headline: Future Mission (2038): What Would You Do?
introScreens.bodyText: Now fast-forward to May 2038. Based on what NASA learned in 2018, if human explorers at Ares Base face a massive 2018-class global dust storm in the future, what would you do? Across 10 challenging Sols, there is always a compromise: protecting Power strains your Crew, and protecting your Crew costs Power—and early choices ripple into later Sols! Watch for highlighted blue words like this to inspect real 2018 NASA facts at any time.
introScreens.nasaSource: Future 2038 Scenario Built From Real Mars Year 34 (2018) Storm Data

kidGlossary.headline: May 30, 2018: Spotted From Mars Orbit
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: On May 30, 2018, NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed a small dust cloud starting near Perseverance Valley. Within days it exploded into a global storm—showing future 2038 crews why orbital satellites give crucial early warning.

kidGlossary.headline: 2018 Storm Towered 37 Miles High
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: In June 2018, high-altitude winds lifted Martian dust over 37 miles (60 km) into the sky—seven times higher than Earth passenger jets fly—hiding even Mars's tallest volcanoes from space cameras.

kidGlossary.headline: Why Opportunity Shut Down in 2018
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Opportunity explored Mars for over 14 years using solar panels. During the June 2018 blackout, sunlight dropped 97%, its batteries went dead in freezing -90°F darkness, and NASA officially declared its mission complete after failing to re-establish contact.

kidGlossary.headline: Curiosity's Nuclear Battery (MMRTG)
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Across the planet from Opportunity, NASA's Curiosity rover never missed a day of science during the 2018 storm because it runs on an MMRTG—a nuclear battery that makes steady electricity from heat instead of sunlight.

kidGlossary.headline: A Martian Sol: 24 Hours, 39 Minutes
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: One day on Mars is called a Sol and lasts 24 hours and 39 minutes. NASA flight controllers on Earth even shifted their sleep schedules to 'Mars Time' during real 2018 rover operations!

kidGlossary.headline: 2018 Physics: 100x Thinner Martian Air
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Mars has 100 times less air than Earth! During the 2018 storm, even 60 mph winds felt like a gentle breeze—so wind won't knock a habitat over, though fine dust still coats solar panels and airlocks.

kidGlossary.headline: 2018 Discovery: Static-Cling Dust
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Martian dust particles are finer than talcum powder and carry static electric charge. In 2018, this microscopic dust clung tightly to Opportunity's solar panels and threatened moving rover joints.

kidGlossary.headline: June 10, 2018: Pitch Black at Noon
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: On June 10, 2018, dust grew so thick above Opportunity that midday on Mars looked darker than a moonlit night on Earth—blocking 97% of the Sun's energy.

kidGlossary.headline: Why Rocket Fuel Must Stay Cryogenic
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: For human Mars return rockets, NASA plans to store super-cold liquid oxygen and methane propellant. Without nonstop electrical coolers, heat leaks in and causes fuel to boil off before astronauts can launch home.

kidGlossary.headline: The 2018 Heat-Blanket Surprise
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Curiosity's REMS weather station proved a strange 2018 twist: while dust storms made Martian days cooler by blocking sunlight, nights got WARMER because the suspended dust acted like a giant blanket trapping surface heat!

kidGlossary.headline: Up to 44-Minute Earth Radio Delay
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: Depending on how far apart Earth and Mars are in their orbits, NASA radio signals take 6 to 22 minutes one way—up to 44 minutes just to ask Mission Control a question and hear back!

kidGlossary.headline: June 20, 2018: Planet-Encircling Dust Event
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: On June 20, 2018, NASA officially classified the storm as a Planet-Encircling Dust Event (PEDE)—one continuous storm blanketing every longitude of Mars at once.

kidGlossary.headline: Lucky 'Cleaning Events' on Real Rovers
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: In earlier years, NASA's Spirit and Opportunity rovers occasionally got rescued when Martian whirlwinds blew dust off their panels—but in 2018 no lucky wind gust saved Opportunity in time.

kidGlossary.headline: Curiosity's Famous June 2018 Selfie
kidGlossary.simpleDefinition: On June 15, 2018, Curiosity snapped a dusty self-portrait inside Gale Crater showing murky orange skies and fine grit across its deck while its nuclear-powered instruments kept measuring the storm.

storyNodes.title: Sol 1: Orbital Storm Alarm
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: On May 30, 2018, NASA orbiters spotted a local dust cloud days before it swallowed the planet.
storyNodes.storyText: Satellites above Ares Base just spotted a small swirling dust storm accelerating toward your landing zone. Right now the sky is clear butterscotch and your solar panels are at peak output every Martian Sol, while your astronauts are outside finishing a critical ice-drilling test.

choiceA.description: Stop all outdoor drilling immediately, bring everyone inside, and pack maximum charge into the main battery vault.
choiceA.outcomeText: You scrub the science dig early and top off your backup batteries. The power grid looks strong, though your crew feels frustrated losing weeks of lab work.

choiceB.description: Keep the team outside to finish collecting ice samples while running compressors hard to fill spare oxygen tanks.
choiceB.outcomeText: The astronauts cheer as they secure priceless ice samples and brim the oxygen tanks, though running pumps hard dips your battery buffer.

storyNodes.title: Sol 2: Dust Hits the Solar Wings
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: By June 3, 2018, fine dust forced NASA's Opportunity team to halt science operations.
storyNodes.storyText: The front edge of the storm reaches Ares Base, climbing more than 37 miles high! Already sticky red grit is clinging to your solar arrays. Your batteries are strong from Sol 1, yet indoor oxygen reserves are dropping faster than expected.

choiceA.buttonLabel: Run Oxygen Makers at Full Power
choiceA.description: Burn stored battery electricity to crack Martian air and ice reserves into fresh breathable oxygen.
choiceA.outcomeText: Fresh oxygen hisses into the habitat and lifts crew energy, though you watch a painful chunk drain off your Sol 1 battery reserve.

choiceB.description: Send astronauts outside in dusty twilight winds to sweep off panels—knowing fine grit can sneak back into the airlock.
choiceB.outcomeText: Sweeping the panels restores solar charging! Still, ultra-fine dust sneaks past the outer seal and leaves two crew members coughing.

storyNodes.title: Sol 2: Red Warning on the Grid
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Martian dust sticks via static electricity—like powder clinging to a balloon.
storyNodes.storyText: Gusts sweep sticky red grit across the landing field while NASA's solar-powered Opportunity rover taught planners how fast sunlight plunges. Your oxygen tanks are full, yet your main battery warning flashes red.

choiceA.description: Cut grow-lights to put your fresh vegetable garden into cold dormancy and feed those amps to base heaters.
choiceA.outcomeText: Turning off the plant bays saves steady power for life support, though losing fresh greens hurts crew nutrition and morale.

choiceB.description: Push your compact nuclear generator above normal safe output to keep both heaters and crops glowing.
choiceB.outcomeText: Electricity surges smoothly into both systems, but safety rules force astronauts to crowd into tight shielding bunks farther from the core.

storyNodes.title: Sol 3: Sky Turns Deep Rust
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Because Mars air is 100x thinner than Earth's, 60 mph winds can't break buildings—but dust blocks the Sun.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Overcharging batteries on Sol 1 kept spare cells ready (+5% Power), though losing early science still dampens crew morale (-5% Crew Health).
storyNodes.storyText: Over half the sunlight has vanished, and outside winds ripple dust dunes even in Mars's ultra-thin air (just read why in highlighted blue words like this). Heating the entire dome is eating power fast.

choiceA.buttonLabel: Seal Side Labs & Cut Hallway Heat
choiceA.description: Shut off outer science rooms and force everyone to bundle inside two central habitat modules.
choiceA.outcomeText: Closing half the base cuts power waste sharply, though freezing frost creeps down unheated corridor walls.

choiceB.description: Spend heavy electricity keeping every workspace warm so astronauts stay active and upbeat.
choiceB.outcomeText: A warm, bright lab restores crew spirits right before the darkest week—at a serious cost to your reserve batteries.

storyNodes.title: Sol 3: Twilight Before Blackout
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: High-altitude dust walls cut midday solar output before total blackout even hits.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Hibernating the greenhouse on Sol 2 kept power wires stable, yet missing fresh food and plant oxygen weighs on crew stamina (-6% Crew Health).
storyNodes.storyText: Dust climbs more than 37 miles high overhead, turning noon into deep amber dusk. Fine powder sneaks into airlock seams even in thin air—forcing a quick choice before solar output hits zero.

choiceA.description: Run electrostatic air curtains at every door to trap gritty dust before it harms crew lungs.
choiceA.outcomeText: Static curtains zap drifting grit out of the doorways! Air stays clean, though your remaining battery bars drop noticeably.

choiceB.buttonLabel: Reroute Grid Power to Weather Sensors
choiceB.description: Cut interior airlock heaters to boost storm radar and save electrical overhead.
choiceB.outcomeText: Your weather computers pull crisp storm telemetry and conserve grid watts, though chilly drafts sweep past the crew bunks.

storyNodes.title: Sol 3: Nuclear Core Carrying the Load
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: In 2018, Curiosity's nuclear battery kept running reliably when solar rovers lost contact.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Extra oxygen filled on Sol 1 gives your crew stronger breathing endurance (+6% Crew Health), while earlier pump loads slightly drained reserves (-5% Power).
storyNodes.storyText: Dust blankets the horizon, yet unlike solar-only explorers, Curiosity kept working thanks to nuclear heat. Your backup fission unit hums loudly—and extra radiator heat builds in the equipment bay.

choiceA.buttonLabel: Move Crew to Narrow Tunnel Shelters
choiceA.description: Save fan power by sealing hot machinery bays and having astronauts sleep in cramped rock tunnels.
choiceA.outcomeText: You conserve vital wattage as the blackout nears, though sleeping shoulder-to-shoulder wears out your astronauts.

choiceB.description: Spend electricity on extra cooling loops so everyone keeps full spacious quarters safely.
choiceB.outcomeText: The nuclear bay cools smoothly and the crew stays comfortable, yet battery reserves shrink right before the blackout.

storyNodes.title: Sol 4: Total Blackout at Noon
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: On June 10, 2018, 97% of sunlight vanished over Opportunity—noon became midnight.
storyNodes.storyText: Midday looks pitch black! The sky blocks 97% of normal sunlight, cutting solar charging to zero. Worse, electric chillers need juice to keep liquid rocket fuel cold so your flight home doesn't boil away!

choiceA.description: Spend precious power on the return rocket chillers while crew members shiver at 50°F inside the hab.
choiceA.outcomeText: Both power and comfort take a hit during peak blackness, yet your homebound rocket propellant stays safely frozen!

choiceB.description: Shut down rocket chillers during the blackout to keep astronauts warm and safe overnight.
choiceB.outcomeText: Warm air circulates through the hab and shields crew health, though warning gauges show propellant warming in the outer tanks.

storyNodes.title: Sol 4: Midnight at Midday
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: NASA instruments discovered dust storms make Mars days colder—yet nights actually get WARMER.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Fine grit tracked in from your Sol 2 spacewalk keeps irritating dry cabin throats during today's blackout (-6% Crew Health).
storyNodes.storyText: Even at high noon, 97% of normal sunlight is blocked. Then weather sensors flash a surprise NASA saw in 2018: suspended dust is trapping heat near the ground, keeping Mars slightly warmer tonight!

choiceA.description: Use the dust blanket's trapped heat to turn down electric heaters and put everyone in insulated suits.
choiceA.outcomeText: Using Mars's own heat blanket saves vital watts for later Sols, though wearing heavy parkas indoors exhausts the crew.

choiceB.buttonLabel: Splurge Power on Hot Meals & Light
choiceB.description: Run kitchen warmers and full cabin lighting to keep crew strength high through the deepest dark.
choiceB.outcomeText: Hot stew and bright lights banish the blackout blues, though your battery telemetry ticks sharply downward.

storyNodes.title: Sol 4: Clogged Scrubbers in the Dark
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Curiosity kept its sensors powered during total darkness while dust coated everything outside.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Overclocking your nuclear unit back on Sol 2 wore down voltage coils—blackout power routing costs an extra reserve penalty today (-6% Power).
storyNodes.storyText: While Curiosity kept working alone in 2018's blackout, your base faces a tougher crisis: sticky red grit just clogged the main cabin air scrubber filter!

choiceA.buttonLabel: Throttle Down Systems to Clean Filters
choiceA.description: Cut base amps temporarily while the crew dons oxygen masks and scrubs every dust filter clean.
choiceA.outcomeText: Breathing masks itch, yet clearing the filters brings crystal-clean cabin air back before anyone gets seriously sick.

choiceB.buttonLabel: Bypass Filter Alarm to Guard Power
choiceB.description: Keep your backup generator roaring at peak output and let dust haze linger inside for another Sol.
choiceB.outcomeText: Your grid stays strongly charged in the pitch dark, yet dusty air leaves astronauts coughing with stinging eyes.

storyNodes.title: Sol 5: Halfway Through the Gloom
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Days after blackout began in 2018, Opportunity slipped into silent low-power fault mode.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Shutting side rooms since Sol 3 keeps conserving amps (+6% Power), though creeping ice along bulkheads saps crew warmth (-6% Crew Health).
storyNodes.storyText: Solar power has now been nearly zero for four whole Sols. Today you must decide whether to reinforce pumps that keep liquid rocket fuel cold or thaw out your crew's frozen medical and gym wing.

choiceA.buttonLabel: Keep Fuel Coolant Pumps at Peak
choiceA.description: Spend heavy electricity stabilizing outer rocket fuel pipes before frost cracks the valves.
choiceA.outcomeText: Valves hold tight without leaking rocket propellant, even as cold stiffness drains everyone indoors.

choiceB.description: Redirect amps inward to warm crew muscles, run physical checkups, and boost hydration.
choiceB.outcomeText: Warm water and stretched muscles revive your tired team, though your battery reserve drops lower.

storyNodes.title: Sol 5: Cabin Fever Under the Blanket
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Global Mars dust storms can trap heat near the ground for weeks without breaking.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Turning off rocket chillers on Sol 4 eased electrical draw today (+4% Power), though astronauts worry about having enough fuel to fly home (-4% Crew Health).
storyNodes.storyText: Outside stays pitch dark even while dust keeps trapping heat near the ground. Five Sols of gloomy twilight are testing your crew's sleep cycles and battery reserves alike.

choiceA.description: Shut down three bunk heaters completely and rotate all four astronauts in one warm core room.
choiceA.outcomeText: Consolidating heat hands a vital boost back to your batteries, though crowded bunk shifts cut deep into rest.

choiceB.description: Spend battery power on sun-lamp therapy and separate bunks so everyone sleeps soundly.
choiceB.outcomeText: Earth-like daylight bulbs lift morale right away, yet the main power gauge slides downward.

storyNodes.title: Sol 5: Dust Haze Inside the Dome
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: On June 15, 2018, Curiosity took a famous selfie coated in dust inside Gale Crater.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Bypassing clogged filters on Sol 4 let fine grit spread into every duct—your astronauts feel weak and short of breath (-6% Crew Health).
storyNodes.storyText: Just like when thick haze coated camera lenses on Curiosity in 2018, fine dust is dulling your sensors inside and out. Your nuclear unit is holding steady, yet crew lungs need help fast.

choiceA.description: Fire up emergency hospital-grade dust vacuums across all habitat rooms.
choiceA.outcomeText: Loud turbines clear the floating grit within hours—saving your crew's lungs at a steep battery cost.

choiceB.description: Save power for exterior storm tracking cameras while issuing dusty filter masks inside.
choiceB.outcomeText: Your base grid builds strength in the dark, though wearing wet paper masks all Sol wears down your astronauts.

storyNodes.title: Sol 6: Alone in Deep Space
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Mars-Earth radio signals take up to 22 minutes one way—44 minutes for a full reply!
storyNodes.storyText: With thick dust blocking communications satellites, every Earth message faces up to a 22-minute radio delay each way. Mission Control asks for a full storm report while your crew quietly fights homesickness.

choiceA.buttonLabel: Boost High-Gain Dish to Call Earth
choiceA.description: Beam full engineering data plus personal family audio across millions of miles of space.
choiceA.outcomeText: Punching a signal through the dust drains big power today, though waiting 40 minutes for family voices to echo back lifts hearts.

choiceB.description: Shut down long-range dish amplifiers completely to hoard every possible watt in the batteries.
choiceB.outcomeText: Power gauges climb out of the danger zone, though silent speakers leave Ares Base feeling painfully cut off from home.

storyNodes.title: Sol 6: The Waiting Game
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: NASA engineers could only send one-way blind commands across millions of miles during the 2018 storm.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Hot meals on Sol 4 helped keep astronaut immune strength high (+5% Crew Health), while extra kitchen heat slightly trimmed reserves (-5% Power).
storyNodes.storyText: Even when thick haze coated camera lenses back in 2018, rovers obeyed Earth commands across a 22-minute radio delay. Today your dish and rover fleet are both pulling standby power.

choiceA.buttonLabel: Put Parked Rovers Into Deep Sleep
choiceA.description: Cut rover battery warmers so every electron stays inside the main astronaut habitat.
choiceA.outcomeText: You pull precious power back into Ares Base, though shutting down backup rovers limits emergency rescue range.

choiceB.description: Use deep-space antenna amps to stream Earth news and entertainment through the storm.
choiceB.outcomeText: Crew smiles return over a movie streamed across Mars's orbit, while reserve meters dip lower.

storyNodes.title: Sol 6: Strain on the Nuclear Bay
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Real nuclear power units (MMRTGs) have zero moving parts, whereas future base turbines must guard against wear.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Heavy sensor loads back on Sol 3 overworked your main voltage bus—fixing corroded contacts eats extra power today (-6% Power).
storyNodes.storyText: Unlike tiny 2018 batteries where Curiosity kept working passively, a full human nuclear system runs hot cooling loops—and yours is groaning while two astronauts struggle with dusty lungs.

choiceA.description: Power down research bays and spend stored amps treating tired astronauts with clean mist.
choiceA.outcomeText: Coughing subsides and heart rates steady, though battery bars dip perilously close to critical.

choiceB.description: Refuse to dial back output, squeezing every kilowatt out of the reactor bay right now.
choiceB.outcomeText: Lights burn bright across Ares Base, yet heat stress and dusty air force one astronaut onto bed rest.

storyNodes.title: Sol 7: Planet-Encircling Dust Event
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: On June 20, 2018, NASA officially declared a Planet-Encircling Dust Event (PEDE).
storyNodes.consequenceText: Reaching Mission Control on Sol 6 paid off—Earth flight surgeons beamed back breathing and morale coaching (+6% Crew Health).
storyNodes.storyText: NASA satellites announce the storm has reached peak spread—a full Planet-Encircling Dust Event! Dust finally stops rising, yet food supplies and water boilers need smart trade-offs.

choiceA.buttonLabel: Serve Cold Ration Bars & Save Water Heat
choiceA.description: Keep kitchen water heaters off and distribute dry emergency ration bricks.
choiceA.outcomeText: Skipping hot cooking saves steady wattage, though chalky ration bars leave your crew sluggish.

choiceB.buttonLabel: Cook Hot Soup & Flush Water Heaters
choiceB.description: Spend a strong burst of electricity to give everyone hot nutrition and clean warm water.
choiceB.outcomeText: Warm broth works wonders for stamina ahead of cleanup Sols, while draining battery reserves again.

storyNodes.title: Sol 7: Dust Stops Climbing
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: On June 20, 2018, dust finally stopped rising—yet heavy skies took weeks to clear.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Holding radio silence on Sol 6 saved valuable amp-hours (+5% Power), though losing contact with home deepened crew stress (-6% Crew Health).
storyNodes.storyText: Sky monitors confirm a full Planet-Encircling Dust Event, just like June 20, 2018! Faint orange light begins returning, and you recall how dust devils swept panels clean for older rovers—though yours are still buried.

choiceA.buttonLabel: Send Crew to Clear Greenhouse Skylights
choiceA.description: Have astronauts step onto the catwalk to sweep dust off upper skylight panels and catch early rays.
choiceA.outcomeText: Dim orange sunlight pierces into the solar bank right away, though stiff joints ache from heavy spacesuits.

choiceB.description: Keep everyone indoors while investing electricity into ultra-pure drinking water recovery.
choiceB.outcomeText: Sparkling clean water refreshes every astronaut, while solar panels stay buried for one more Sol.

storyNodes.title: Sol 7: Medical Alert in the Gloom
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Astronaut safety limits mean humans cannot simply 'wait it out' like a dormant robot.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Skipping air scrubbing earlier allowed suspended dust to choke cabin vents—astronauts now need supplemental oxygen (-6% Crew Health).
storyNodes.storyText: Even while thick haze coated camera lenses on Curiosity without hurting a robot, human lungs inside Ares Base are struggling badly! You must spend serious reserves on medical recovery or risk collapse.

choiceA.description: Burn heavy reserves running medical oxygen concentrators and full habitat air scrubbers.
choiceA.outcomeText: Emergency medical scrubbers rescue your astronauts cleanly—leaving battery banks nearly emptied.

choiceB.buttonLabel: Hold Power & Issue Sealed Oxygen Helmets
choiceB.description: Save electrical reserves and order exhausted crew members to wear heavy helmets indoors.
choiceB.outcomeText: Your grid holds plenty of charge, yet wearing clunky space helmets around the clock drives crew health toward red alert.

storyNodes.title: Sol 8: Digging Out the Solar Farm
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Waiting solely on Martian winds failed Opportunity in 2018—human crews can act directly.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Keeping return rocket propellant frozen since Sol 4 requires extra compressor draw again today (-6% Power), keeping your Earth rocket ready.
storyNodes.storyText: Dust settles visibly out of the upper sky! NASA once hoped lucky dust devils swept panels clean on 2018 rovers, yet a heavy blanket of red grit still covers your huge solar wings.

choiceA.description: Send astronauts outside in cleared dusk light with anti-static brushes to uncover Wing Array 1.
choiceA.outcomeText: Sunlight pours back onto freshly swept solar glass! Your crew returns exhausted and caked in dust.

choiceB.description: Let tired astronauts recover inside while balancing aging battery cells with remaining nuclear amps.
choiceB.outcomeText: Rest heals aching backs and eases stress, though leaving panels dusty wastes precious returning sunlight.

storyNodes.title: Sol 8: Returning Sunlight
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Solar recovery after a global storm depends on clearing static-charged dust from glass cells.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Sweeping skylights on Sol 7 already pulls extra midday charge (+5% Power), though your outdoor crew nurses stiff muscles (-5% Crew Health).
storyNodes.storyText: Now that 60% less sky is choked by storm grit, engineers debate how to shed static dust without hoping that dust devils swept panels clean like in 2018.

choiceA.description: Fire vibrating frame shakers across the solar arrays—noisy vibrations rock the whole habitat floor.
choiceA.outcomeText: Clouds of dust slide cleanly off the arrays! Constant metallic rattling frays everyone's sleep indoors.

choiceB.description: Use steady electricity to humidify scratchy cabin air and give astronauts a full unbroken sleep cycle.
choiceB.outcomeText: Deep restful sleep transforms your team's readiness, while your power reserves shrink closer to low warning.

storyNodes.title: Sol 8: Cooling Pump Burnout
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Real space power hardware needs safety margins rather than continuous redline operation.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Pushing the nuclear backup to redline on Sol 6 scorched a pump seal—switching to auxiliary cooling costs power today (-8% Power).
storyNodes.storyText: Unlike Curiosity's rock-solid passive battery where Curiosity kept working effortlessly, your overworked cooling loop just blew a gasket—just as the skies begin clearing!

choiceA.description: Commit remaining reserve juice to healing exhausted astronauts before launch preparations begin.
choiceA.outcomeText: Sick bay oxygen restores weakened crew members fast, while pushing base power dangerously low.

choiceB.description: Spend remaining grid juice launching an atmospheric balloon to save scientific value despite crew fatigue.
choiceB.outcomeText: Your balloon captures priceless storm-clearing physics data for NASA, while exhausting an already weary crew.

storyNodes.title: Sol 9: Preparing the Return Rocket
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: By July 2018, NASA still listened daily for Opportunity's wake-up signal as skies slowly cleared.
storyNodes.consequenceText: Because astronauts swept solar Wing 1 on Sol 8, bright sunlight refills batteries rapidly (+7% Power), though crews need extra rest and electrolytes (-4% Crew Health).
storyNodes.storyText: The butterscotch sky is brightening fast! Back in 2018, NASA's solar-powered Opportunity rover never woke up as dust settled—so Ares Base must carefully balance battery recharge and astronaut readiness.

choiceA.description: Spend incoming solar power splitting ice into fresh drinking water and pure oxygen for the crew.
choiceA.outcomeText: Crew health bounces back as crisp oxygen and fresh water fill every tap across the base.

choiceB.description: Work the exhausted crew overtime testing fuel chillers so Ares Base maximizes electrical readiness.
choiceB.outcomeText: Solar inverters charge rocket systems nicely, though long checklists drain astronaut energy ahead of the final Sol.

storyNodes.title: Sol 9: Clearing Skies, Hidden Ice
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: As dust settled in July 2018, Mars cooled rapidly at night without its dust blanket.
storyNodes.storyText: With dust dropping away, Mars loses the heat blanket from trapping heat near the ground—turning nights freezing -90°F again! Exterior radiator fins need defrosting before Sol 10.

choiceA.buttonLabel: Spacewalk to Chip Frost Off Radiators
choiceA.description: Send suited astronauts outside in brutal -90°F night chill to clear exterior heat exchangers.
choiceA.outcomeText: Clean radiator fins boost power efficiency strongly, though icy fingers and frostbite warnings stress the team.

choiceB.buttonLabel: Keep Crew Inside for Full Medical Exams
choiceB.description: Spend extra electric heat indoors while doctors check lungs and muscles across all four astronauts.
choiceB.outcomeText: Full checkups restore astronaut readiness across the board, while your batteries take another clear hit.

storyNodes.title: Sol 9: Survival Mode Recovery
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: After long communication gaps, NASA always runs cautious system health diagnostics first.
storyNodes.storyText: Even across a shrinking 22-minute radio delay, Mission Control sees Ares Base's warning lights glowing amber. You have one Sol left before Earth evaluates whether the base survived intact.

choiceA.buttonLabel: Seal & Sanitize Airlocks for Crew Health
choiceA.description: Pour remaining power into deep cabin cleaning and medical rest for your weary team.
choiceA.outcomeText: Air clears and exhausted crew members rally, though power meters drop toward emergency minimum.

choiceB.description: Finish uploading your priceless storm science dataset while locking emergency pod latches.
choiceB.outcomeText: Mission Control receives full storm science, though pushing on empty leaves both crew and grid strained.

storyNodes.title: Sol 10: Dawn After the Storm
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Global storms subside slowly over weeks—final system reboots require strict discipline.
storyNodes.storyText: Sunlight pours onto Ares Base for the first clear morning of your 10th Martian Sol! With one final compromise left, decide where to push your final surge before Earth logs your 2038 storm grade.

choiceA.buttonLabel: Lock Launch Rocket Power & Charge Vault
choiceA.description: Work the crew hard through a full 12-hour exterior diagnostic to recharge rocket and battery banks.
choiceA.outcomeText: Fuel chillers and battery vaults lock into green zone—though your astronauts finish soaked in sweat.

choiceB.description: Spend remaining battery charge reviving fresh food bays and giving astronauts a restful feast.
choiceB.outcomeText: Astronauts celebrate the dawn around newly lit green sprouts—at one final cost to electrical storage.

storyNodes.title: Sol 10: Final System Check
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Opportunity had over 1,000 silent check-ins before NASA closed the mission—reserves decide survival.
storyNodes.storyText: Skies match bright butterscotch once more, recalling how NASA's solar-powered Opportunity rover met its fate when power hit bottom. Make one last careful compromise before final Mission Control review!

choiceA.description: Order astronauts into gritty spacesuits one last time to reset dusty exterior power inverters.
choiceA.outcomeText: Main meters climb sharply as clean solar amps refill the grid, draining crew strength at the finish line.

choiceB.description: Use battery power indoors to flush dust from cabin air and stabilize crew vital signs.
choiceB.outcomeText: Doctor monitors flash steady green across all four astronauts while power gauges dip down.

storyNodes.title: Sol 10: Emergency Rescue Hold
storyNodes.nasaFactBanner: 2018 LESSON: Early storm warnings in 2018 showed why reserves cannot dip to zero during blackout weeks.
storyNodes.storyText: Even though satellites gave warning back when they spotted a small swirling dust storm, Ares Base enters Sol 10 on fumes. Pick what to save in the final hour!

choiceA.description: Empty remaining battery cells directly into astronaut breathing and thermal blankets.
choiceA.outcomeText: You keep every astronaut breathing safely until skies clear, sacrificing base machinery reserves.

choiceB.description: Cut cabin comforts completely to rescue base electronics and keep orbital beacons transmitting.
choiceB.outcomeText: Beacons ping cleanly back to Mars orbit, while frozen crews hunker down in emergency sleep pods.

endings.headline: Sol 10: Mission Success — The NASA Blueprint!
endings.storyText: Sunlight floods Ares Base once again! Through smart compromises across 10 grueling Sols, your solar arrays, nuclear unit, and return rocket fuel stayed intact—and all four astronauts are healthy and ready to keep exploring Mars.

endings.headline: Sol 10: Safe Crew, Extra Fuel Delivery Needed
endings.storyText: All four astronauts came through the 2038 monster storm healthy! However, protecting crew comfort during the blackout forced fuel coolers offline—so NASA must send an uncrewed tanker rocket before your team can fly home.

endings.headline: Sol 10: Base Intact, Exhausted Crew
endings.storyText: Your solar wings, battery banks, and return rocket survived the 10-Sol blackout without a scratch—but constant rationing, dust exposure, and cold corridors pushed the crew to their limit. Mission Control orders weeks of strict medical rest.

endings.headline: Sol 10: The Opportunity Rover Fate
endings.storyText: Just like NASA's solar-powered Opportunity rover back in 2018, reserves dropped too low during the blackout. Emergency survival pods kept astronauts safe until a rescue lander arrived—proving why future bases need deep safety margins!

realLifeComparison.title: Compare Your Future 2038 Mission to Real 2018 NASA Science

cards.whatHappenedInRealLife: In June 2018, NASA's solar-powered Opportunity rover lost 97% of its sunlight, couldn't recharge, and froze in the dark after 14 years on Mars. Across the planet, Curiosity kept working right through the storm because it carried a small nuclear battery (an MMRTG).
cards.howItConnectsToGame: NASA's future Mars bases plan to combine solar arrays with small nuclear fission reactors—just like your 2038 base needed both to survive 10 Sols!

cards.whatHappenedInRealLife: NASA's weather station on Curiosity discovered something surprising: while 2018 dust storms made Mars days cooler by blocking sunlight, they made Mars nights WARMER because dust trapped heat near the ground.
cards.howItConnectsToGame: Midway through the storm, dialing down heaters worked because suspended red dust acted like a giant blanket over Mars.

cards.whatHappenedInRealLife: Because Mars is millions of miles away, radio messages in 2018 took 6 to 22 minutes each way—up to 44 minutes just to ask a question and get an answer.
cards.howItConnectsToGame: Every compromise you made had ripple effects days later—just like real astronauts must survive on their own choices before Earth even knows!
